nameStory: The Least Flycatcher gets its name from being the smallest member of the Empidonax flycatcher group in eastern North America. It's also called 'chebec' or 'chebecker' after its distinctive call that sounds exactly like someone saying 'che-BEK!' with sharp emphasis on the second syllable.
description: The Least Flycatcher is a small, olive-brown songbird that makes its living catching insects on the wing. About the size of a chickadee, it has a fairly large head, a short neck, and a relatively big bill for snatching flying bugs. Like other flycatchers, it sits upright on exposed perches and darts out to grab prey before returning to the same spot. Its overall appearance is quite plain - grayish-olive above and whitish below with subtle wing bars.

idTips.label: Che-BEK Call
idTips.description: Listen for the sharp, two-note 'che-BEK!' call that sounds like someone snapping out a command - this is by far the best way to identify this species

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more compact than other Empidonax flycatchers, with a proportionally larger head that gives it an almost big-headed appearance

idTips.label: Whitish Wing Bars
idTips.description: Two crisp, white wing bars that stand out against the olive-brown wings, often appearing bright white in good light

idTips.label: Eye Ring
idTips.description: Thin but distinct white eye ring that makes the dark eye appear larger and more prominent against the grayish face

idTips.label: Upright Posture
idTips.description: Sits very erect on exposed branches with bill pointed slightly upward, ready to launch after flying insects

idTips.label: Short Bill
idTips.description: Bill appears shorter and less pointed than other Empidonax flycatchers, though still wide at the base for catching insects

habitat: Look for Least Flycatchers in open deciduous and mixed woodlands, especially forest edges, clearings, and young second-growth areas throughout New England. They prefer areas with scattered trees and open spaces for hunting insects, often near streams or ponds. You'll commonly find them in parks, large yards with mature trees, and along woodland trails where they can perch on exposed branches.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in late April to early May when males begin their persistent 'che-BEK' calling from prominent perches to establish territory and attract mates.
seasonality.summer: Most active and vocal during breeding season, with frequent calling and visible fly-catching behavior as they feed young.
seasonality.fall: Becomes much quieter in August and September before migrating south, making identification more challenging without the distinctive call.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England, spending winter in Central America and northern South America.

funFact: A single Least Flycatcher can snap up over 1,000 flying insects in a single day during peak summer feeding, and they're so precise that they can catch tiny gnats while completely ignoring larger, harmless insects that aren't worth the energy expenditure.
confusionNotes: The Empidonax flycatchers are notoriously difficult to tell apart by sight alone - the 'che-BEK' call is absolutely essential for confident identification. Without the call, focus on the Least's smaller size, more compact build, and shorter bill compared to Alder and Willow Flycatchers. Remember: 'Least calls the least complex' - just two sharp syllables.
contextualKnowledge: The Empidonax genus is famous among birders for being one of the most challenging identification groups in North America, often called 'Empids' for short. Even experienced birders rely heavily on vocalizations rather than visual features to distinguish between species in this group.
compareHints: Among its Empidonax cousins in New England, the Least Flycatcher is noticeably smaller and more compact than Alder and Willow Flycatchers, with a proportionally larger head and shorter bill. Yellow-bellied Flycatchers have more yellowish underparts and prefer wetter, more coniferous habitats, while Acadian Flycatchers are larger with longer bills and prefer mature deciduous forests. When in doubt, let their voices be your guide - each species has a distinctive call.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Empidonax flycatchers, Alder Flycatchers are most easily separated by voice rather than appearance.
Among New England's Empidonax flycatchers, willow flycatchers are most easily confused with alder flycatchers—voice is the key difference.

Among its Empidonax relatives, the yellow-bellied flycatcher is the only one with truly yellow underparts – Least Flycatchers are grayish-white below, while Alder and Willow Flycatchers are whitish with just a hint of yellow.
Among the Empidonax flycatchers, Acadians are the most olive-green above, while Least Flycatchers are grayer and Yellow-bellied Flycatchers are more uniformly yellowish below.
Compared to other Empidonax flycatchers in New England, the Western Flycatcher has a more distinctly teardrop-shaped eye ring and brighter orange-yellow lower mandible.
Among Empidonax flycatchers, Hammond's shows the most peaked crown and does less tail-flicking than Least Flycatcher.
